title: Arrowroot
wiki_lead:
Arrowroot is a starch obtained from the rhizomes (rootstock) of several tropical plants, traditionally in particular Maranta arundinacea, but also Florida arrowroot (Zamia integrifolia), as well as tapioca from cassava (Manihot esculenta), which is often labeled arrowroot. In Kenya, "arrowroot" refers to nduma, a plant known elsewhere as taro. Polynesian arrowroot or pia (Tacca leontopetaloides), Guyana arrowroot (Dioscorea alata), Japanese arrowroot or kudzu (Pueraria lobata), and purple arrowroot (Canna indica) are used in similar ways.

M. arundinacea is called ପାଳୁଅ (paḷua) in Odisha, India, and uraró/araró in the Philippines, where it is the base starch of a popular cookie.

History
Archaeological studies in the Americas show evidence of arrowroot cultivation as early as 7,000 years ago. The name may come from aru-aru (meal of meals) in the language of the Caribbean Arawak people, for whom the plant was a staple. It has also been suggested that the name comes from arrowroot's use in treating poison-arrow wounds, as it draws out the poison when applied to the site of the injury.
In the early days of carbonless copy paper, arrowroot starch, because of its appropriate grain-size, was a widely used ingredient. After an economical way of centrifugally separating wheat flour was devised, arrowroot lost its role in papermaking.


Uses


Cultivation in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

Saint Vincent has a long history of arrowroot production. The industry started as the food and medicine of the Carib and Garifuna peoples and developed to the status of a major export of St. Vincent during the period 1900 to 1965. It became an important commodity in colonial trade in the 1930s. As the sugar industry declined in the nineteenth century, cultivation of arrowroot was developed to fill the void. Since then, the area cultivated has declined steadily as other crops, particularly bananas, have gained wider acceptance by farmers. Evidence of its former importance is indicated by the ruins of the various magnificent 19th-century factories located in valleys on the St. Vincent mainland.
Arrowroot cultivation is now concentrated on farms located north of the Rabacca River, particularly in the Owia area. This is also the area where the population of Carib descent is concentrated. In 1998/99, the industry produced 312,000 lb (142,000 kg) of starch, about 3% of the peak level in the 1960s.

In the past, the St. Vincent arrowroot industry played an important role in the economy of the island, contributing close to 50% of the country's foreign export earnings, and was the principal source of employment and income of the rural people from the 1930s to the 1960s.

The plant is propagated from rhizomes and cultivation takes place at elevations up to 300 metres on the eastern and windward facing side of the highlands of St. Vincent. Cultivation covers an area of about 3,700 ha and some 80% of the crop is grown by small farmers. The arrowroot plant is very hardy and not very demanding in its requirements. St. Vincent, particularly the north-east coast, provides the ideal growing conditions for optimal yields: deep, well drained, slightly acidic soils and a hot, humid climate. Some farmers produce the crop by shifting cultivation on the cleared forested slopes.

The harvesting season extends from October to May. On the larger estates, the harvesting of the rhizome usually proceeds from the base of a hill towards the top. Harvesting involves breaking off the rhizome from the shoot. Planting and harvesting are inter-related in that when the rhizomes are harvested the shoot is replanted at the same time. In St. Vincent, much use is made of rural unemployment, and many women workers are involved in the various phases of operation. Mechanical harvesters have recently been introduced, allowing faster arrowroot harvesting.
Six factories process the island's arrowroot and large processing plants are located at Belle Vue and at Owia.

grok_lead: Arrowroot is a fine, white starch powder extracted from the rhizomes of Maranta arundinacea, a perennial herbaceous plant in the Marantaceae family native to the tropical regions of Central and South America, including the West Indies. The plant features erect stems growing up to 1.5 meters (5 feet) tall with large, ovate leaves and white flowers, thriving in the moist understory of evergreen or deciduous forests. Its rhizomes, which spread horizontally underground, contain high levels of easily digestible starch, making arrowroot a valuable food source historically cultivated by indigenous peoples such as the Arawak for sustenance and wound treatment. Maranta arundinacea has been domesticated since prehistoric times, with evidence of its use dating back thousands of years in the Americas for both nutritional and medicinal purposes. The name "arrowroot" originates from its traditional application by South American indigenous groups to treat arrow wounds, believed to neutralize poisons due to its soothing properties. European colonizers later recognized its potential, introducing it to other tropical areas like Indonesia and Australia for commercial starch production, where it remains an underutilized crop despite its adaptability to various soils. Today, major production occurs in countries such as Brazil, Guyana, Fiji, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, involving harvesting mature rhizomes, washing, pulping, and sieving to yield the pure starch. The starch's neutral taste, clarity when cooked, and stability under heat and acidity make it a preferred thickener in culinary applications, including sauces, puddings, gluten-free baking, and infant foods, where its high digestibility provides nutritional benefits without causing digestive distress. Beyond food, arrowroot finds use in pharmaceuticals as a binder, in cosmetics for its absorbent qualities, and in industrial products like paper and textiles due to its binding properties. With a nutritional profile rich in carbohydrates (about 80-90% starch) but low in protein and fat, it serves as a hypoallergenic alternative to cornstarch or wheat flour, supporting its growing demand in health-conscious and vegan markets.
